## Overview

The Chamorro people, also called Chamoru, are the Indigenous people of the Mariana Islands, politically divided between Guam and the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands in Micronesia. According to the 2020 census, about 63,035 people with Chamorro ancestry lived in Guam and another 17,163 in the Northern Marianas; significant populations also live in several United States states. Chamorro belongs to the Austronesian family and is generally placed within the Malayo-Polynesian subgroup. The people are associated with expert seafaring, intricate weaving, detailed pottery-making, matrilineal social organization, distinctive cuisine, dance, oral traditions, and a language shaped by centuries of Spanish influence. Chamorro culture also reflects Spanish, Mexican, American, Japanese, Filipino, German, and other Oceanic influences.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

*Intricate weaving* is named in the sources as one of the craft skills associated with early Chamorros.

### Clothing & dress

Before Spanish contact, Chamorro boys and men went fully nude. Chamorro girls also went nude until around the age of eight to ten, when they began wearing a small genital covering made from bark, leaves, turtle shell, or, in some cases, matting. Both sexes sometimes wore hats made from woven leaves to protect themselves from the sun.

Chamorro women were associated with teeth blackening or dental lacquering, which was considered beautiful and distinguished them from animals. A record also describes “penis pins” as a chastity measure for young males. In later traditional dance dress, women wore *mestizas* dresses, while men wore a *sadí* made from cotton or linen.

### Architecture

The *latte stone* is a megalithic rock pillar topped with a hemispherical capstone. Early Chamorros used latte stones as foundations for buildings, and the form was later appropriated as a national symbol. The sources also describe a creation tradition in which Fu'una transformed herself into a giant rock; proposed locations for this rock include a site at a church in Agat and Laso de Fua in Fouha Bay in Umatac.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Early Chamorros are described as skilled in detailed pottery-making. The sources also mention traditional wooden sticks used in dance and outrigger canoes used for war, fishing, and sailing. No metalworking tradition or named household object is documented.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The sources describe hair and dental practices rather than jewelry. Early European accounts reported that Chamorro people wore long black hair down to the waist or farther, while another account described hair tied into one or two topknots. Around 1670, a Catholic missionary reported a hairstyle in which the head was shaved except for a “finger-length” amount of hair at the crown. Chamorro women practiced teeth blackening or dental lacquering, and young males were described as using “penis pins.”

## Music & performance

They do describe singing within a Chamorro legend: when men could not catch a gigantic fish that was eating away at Guam, women used their hair to weave a net, and the net grew larger as they sang. Their singing enchanted the fish and drew it into the net.

Chamorro performance traditions include chant, dance, and storytelling. The Chamoru dance is described as connected with these cultural practices, and Chamorro dance instructors have led *Guma* groups in several United States states. The sources also describe a dance movement shaped by a canoe. Chamorros practiced this movement, called *galaidé*, through hand movements or by using traditional wooden sticks.

## Dance & theatre

Chamorro dance is associated with chant, dance, and storytelling. A *Guma* may be led by Chamorro dance instructors who belonged to historical Guam dance groups. Chamorro dance costumes were traditionally woven and crafted: women wore *mestizas* dresses and men wore a *sadí* made from cotton or linen.

A significant dance movement is traditionally shaped by a canoe. The *galaidé* was practiced through hand movements or with traditional wooden sticks. The sources connect the canoe with war, fishing, and sailing in ancient times.

## Festivals & rituals

They do, however, describe several ritual and ceremonial practices. Ancient Chamorros engaged in ancestor veneration, while some residents of the Marianas still ask permission from ancestral spirits before entering parts of jungles. Most Chamorros are Roman Catholic, although some customs and beliefs from before the first European conquests continue.

Chamorro cuisine is associated with special events including parties called *gupot* or “fiestas,” *nobenas*, and high-school or college graduations. Liberation Day commemorates the recapture of Guam by American forces on July 21, 1944.

## Foodways

Chamorro cuisine reflects Spanish, Filipino, Korean, Chinese, Japanese, American, and other influences. Rice was cultivated in the Marianas since prehistory. Red rice made with *achoti* is a distinct staple and is strongly associated with Chamorro cuisine. It is commonly served at special events such as *gupot* or “fiestas,” *nobenas*, and high-school or college graduations. The condiment *fina'denne'* accompanies most meals.

Named foods include *kelaguen*, in which meat is denatured partly or entirely by citric acid rather than heat; *tinaktak*, a meat dish made with coconut milk; and *kå'du fanihi*, a flying fox or fruit bat soup. Fruits used in local recipes include *lemmai*, *mangga*, *niyok*, and *bilimbines*. Local cookies are called *guyuria*. Foreign-origin foods include sweet or savory *empanada* from Spain and *pancit* from the Philippines. Spanish settlement in the 17th century introduced cattle and contributed to dishes such as *tinala' katne*. Spam and other canned meats were introduced after World War II and contributed to a dietary shift.

## Oral tradition & literature

Chamorro oral tradition includes a creation story about the celestial siblings Puntan and Fu'una. Puntan’s body became parts of the universe: his eyes became the Sun and Moon, his eyebrows became rainbows, and other body parts became features of the Earth. Fu'una brought the sun, soil, and waters to life, transformed into stone, and gave birth to the Chamorro people. The story changed over time as it passed from one generation to another.

The tradition also includes *Taotaomo'na*, spirits of ancient Chamorros, and *Birak*, a broader term that can refer to the undead, demons, or general elemental types. *Taotaomona* refers to “people of early times” and to ancestral spirits believed in by Chamorros and some neighboring islanders from Rota and Saipan. These spirits can cause sickness and death to those who offend them, and their appearance may be female or male, attractive or monstrous.

Contemporary preservation efforts include Chamorro immersion schools, smartphone applications, internet videos, television programs, dictionaries, and the soap opera *Siha*. The sources also mention *Nihi! Kids*, a program intended to perpetuate Chamoru language and culture.

## Language & religion

Chamorro is an Austronesian language, generally classified within the Malayo-Polynesian family. It has three distinct dialects: Guamanian, Rotanese, and the dialect of the other Northern Mariana Islands. Chamorro has acquired many Spanish loanwords after more than 300 years of Spanish colonization, and Spanish influence includes vocabulary, numerals, verbs, articles, prepositions, and conjunctions. The language has 24 phonemes, including 18 consonants and six vowels.

Chamorro is threatened by a decline in fluency. In Guam, the United States government banned Chamorro in schools and workplaces in 1922. After World War II, “no Chamorro” restrictions continued in local schools. Public schools on Guam and in the Northern Marianas are now required by law to teach Chamorro, and revitalization efforts include immersion schools and the 2021 *Utgrafihan CHamoru* spelling standard released by Guam’s *Kumisión I Fino' CHamoru*.

Most Chamorros are Roman Catholic. Earlier practices included ancestor veneration, and some residents continue to seek permission from ancestral spirits before entering parts of jungles. Traditional healers called *suruhånu*, or *suruhåna* for women, are respected for their knowledge of herbal treatments and spirits.
